ETF: Exchange-traded fund: one security that holds a basket of many others (shares or bonds) and trades on an exchange like a share.
TER: Total expense ratio: the fund's yearly running cost as a % of your money. It is taken out of the fund's price every day, so you never see a bill.
Accumulating: The fund reinvests the dividends it receives instead of paying them out. In Italy you pay tax only when you sell.
Distributing: The fund pays dividends or coupons out to you. Each payment is taxed when you receive it.
Savings plan: An automatic purchase of the same amount at a set interval (for example every month). On Trade Republic it has no order fee.
Benchmark: What a fund or a paper strategy is compared with. In Explore it is often a world ETF; in the Trading Lab it is the Europe ETF held on paper. If something cannot beat it after costs, the simple choice would have done better.
Worst drop: The largest fall from a high point to the lowest point that followed (also called maximum drawdown). It shows how bad things got, not how often.
Volatility: How much the price typically swings in a year. 15% means a normal year can easily move about 15% up or down.
Overlap: The share of two funds' money that sits in the same companies. Two world ETFs often overlap by more than 80%: owning both adds little.
Currency exposure: Which currencies your companies earn and are priced in. A world ETF bought in euros is still mostly exposed to the US dollar.
Stamp duty: Italy's imposta di bollo: by law 0.20% a year of the value of your securities. Trade Republic's Italian help page says none is applied to the securities account, so SV Terminal shows both figures until this is settled.
Capital gains tax: In Italy 26% of your gain when you sell (12.5% on the government-bond part of bond funds). Trade Republic withholds it for Italian residents.
Cost basis: What you paid for what you hold. For the Italian tax on an ETF gain the order fees are not part of it (they create a small loss credit instead); for shares and ETCs they are.
Money-weighted return: Your personal yearly return, taking into account when you put money in and took it out (XIRR). Two people in the same fund can have very different ones.
Rebalancing: Bringing a portfolio back to the weights chosen for it, for example by directing new money to what is under its target.
